Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit of a situation at work. I've been a retail supervisor for years, you know, and I usually run a tight ship. I've got a degree, I know how to manage people, but lately... well, my wife actually made this appointment because of what's been happening when I try to run the floor. 

See, I came in because when I try to explain the inventory numbers to the team, or even just lay out the weekend schedule—which shouldn't be hard, I've done it a thousand times—my words just start jumping all over the place. Like, I'll start off talking about the delivery trucks coming in, which is normal, right? We have to prep for the trucks. But then my brain just skips, and suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, and then for some reason I'm going on and on about the church grill from the picnic last month, and then I'm analyzing my boss’s tone of voice from a phone call we had... all in the exact same breath. 

And I look at my staff, these young kids mostly, and they're just staring at me. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I’m saying. It’s like they’re watching a movie with the sound out of sync or something. And I try to pull it back, because there are so many details I need them to know about the stockroom and the weekend rush, but the words just keep colliding. It's incredibly frustrating, to be honest, because I know exactly what I want to communicate in my head, but it just comes out as this avalanche of things that don't belong together, and I can't seem to stop it once it starts.

Hear or see things? Like... like things that aren't real? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I understand why you're asking, trying to rule things out and all that, but no, my eyes and ears work perfectly fine. It's all very real. Very solid. I'm not seeing shadows or hearing voices or anything like that. 

Even going back to that Sunday morning with my wife, the one I told you about... I was looking right at the oak tree in the front yard. I was looking at the actual, physical leaves clogging up the aluminum gutters. There wasn't anything imaginary floating around. Just the tree, my coffee cup, the kitchen table, the morning news playing on the television in the background. So, no, I've never had anything like that happen. It's strictly just the words coming out of my mouth that get tangled. But as far as taking in the world around me? I see and hear exactly what everybody else sees and hears. Nothing extra. Just the usual daily chaos, you know? The squeaky wheels on the shopping carts, the terrible pop music on the overhead speakers... all very, very real.

Memory? Oh, no. No, no trouble there at all. In fact, my memory is probably one of my best assets. You have to have a steel-trap memory in retail, doctor, you really do, or the whole operation just falls apart on you. 

Just on Tuesday—because Wednesday was the vendor delivery, so it had to be Tuesday—I was doing the cycle counts for the electronics department. Well, doctor, I feel like we might be covering the same ground here, because, like I was just saying a minute ago, when I am entirely alone with my thoughts? Sitting in my office, door closed, reviewing the weekly metrics? No, not at all. My thoughts don't race. They don't feel disjointed or chaotic. You can see it in their eyes, this total, utter confusion, like I've suddenly started speaking Greek or something. They're waiting for instructions on where to put the patio umbrellas, and I'm giving them this word salad about church hotdogs and delivery schedules. It's incredibly frustrating for me, and I know it's confusing for them. But if I'm just sitting quietly by myself? No, everything is perfectly orderly. It's strictly the speaking part that's the problem.

That's exactly why I'm sitting in this chair right now. If it was just a little quirk, I'd brush it off, but... yes, it is absolutely affecting my job, and frankly, my whole life. \n\nYou know how retail works, the weekends are your bread and butter. Saturdays and Sundays are when you make or break your sales goals for the entire week, and I have run those weekend shifts for over a decade. They took me off them completely. They've got me working Tuesday mornings, which is practically a ghost town. Suspended! He said if things don't improve, if I can't communicate clearly with the floor staff without confusing everybody, they're going to have to put me on unpaid leave. At my age, with my degree and my track record, the thought of being suspended is just humiliating. I mean, I'm a supervisor. I'm supposed to be the one keeping things organized.\n\nAnd it’s not just the store, either, which is the really hard part to swallow. It’s bleeding into everything else. My wife... she’s a saint, really, but she’s had to start covering all these commitments I used to handle without batting an eye. I'd start talking to the guy fixing our water heater, and suddenly he's looking at me like I have two heads, or I'd be at the HOA meeting and people would just sort of slowly back away from the conversation. Well, see, that’s the thing, doctor. That’s the really tricky part about all of this. So I’m very attuned to faces. And when I’m talking, feeling perfectly fine, perfectly in control, and suddenly I see my cashier—like young Jason who works the front registers—when I see his eyebrows knit together and he gets this sort of glassy, deer-in-the-headlights stare... that’s when I get frustrated. Not anxious, really, just... profoundly irritated and confused myself. Because I’m looking at him and thinking, 'Why aren't you understanding this incredibly simple instruction about the promotional signage?' \n\nI just don't get why they look at me like that. We get these massive shipments of charging cables, earbuds, phone cases, and the computerized inventory system is always, and I mean *always*, off by a few units because of shrink or cashiers mis-scanning items at the front registers. But I can tell you exactly how many units of the six-foot braided charging cables we had on peg hook number four. I can remember that Jason called out sick last Friday because his alternator died, and I had to pull Sarah from housewares to cover the registers, even though she hates working the registers because she says the scanner glare gives her a headache. I remember all of the schedules, all the product placements, all of it. \n\nMy wife even jokes about it. My head feels perfectly clear, but the words... it's just the words that get tangled up. It's like I'm speaking a foreign language to them, even though I'm just trying to explain the schedule! So internally, no, my thoughts are a perfectly straight line. It's just... the translation from my brain to my mouth that seems to be putting everything in a blender.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your thoughts are racing or disjointed when you're alone with your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I feel like we might be covering the same ground here, because, like I was just saying a minute ago, when I am entirely alone with my thoughts? Well, that’s the thing, isn't it? When I'm just sitting by myself, when it's just me and my own brain, everything feels perfectly fine. The thoughts are all there, lined up exactly how they should be. But... the moment I actually open my mouth to try and communicate them, that's when the wheels completely fall off the wagon.

But as I started talking, my words just... they started jumping all over the place. 

I started out talking about the delivery trucks, which made sense, but then suddenly I was talking about Thursdays, because the trucks usually come on Thursdays, and then that made me think about the church grill we used last Thursday for the parish picnic, and before I knew it, I was rambling on about the tone my district manager used on our last conference call. And I could see it on Greg's face. He was just staring at me, you know? That look people give you when they have absolutely no idea how to follow what you're saying, like you're speaking a foreign language or you've completely lost the plot. 

And the frustrating part is, in my head, the connection between the inventory, the trucks, the schedule, and my boss makes perfect sense! It’s all part of the same stressful situation. But when it comes out of my mouth, it just... it doesn't connect for anyone else. It's like I'm trying to hand someone a neatly organized stack of papers, but right as I hand it over, a gust of wind blows them all over the room, and they're just left holding one random page about a church grill while I'm trying to explain payroll. So, internally? No, the thoughts aren't disconnected at all. But the translation from my brain to my mouth... that's where the breakdown is happening, and it's making me look like I don't know how to run my own store.

Everything else upstairs is working exactly the way it always has, sharp as a tack.\n\nDoctor: Did you notice any changes in your behavior, mood, or the way you think before you started having these problems with your speech?\n\nPatient: Changes in my mood or behavior... well, you know, it's funny you ask about the timeline, because I've actually thought a lot about when this all started creeping up on me. It hasn't just been a sudden thing, like flipping a light switch. No, this has been building for, oh, I’d say about eleven months now. And I can pinpoint it pretty accurately because that’s exactly when corporate decided to restructure our region and they brought in this new district manager. \n\nHe came in, and suddenly everything we’ve been doing perfectly well for the last decade just wasn't good enough anymore. He started pushing us—and I mean really pushing—on our quarterly forecasts and our labor schedules. Used to be, I could write the floor schedule two weeks out, account for my full-timers, give the college kids their weekend hours, and we were golden. We ran a tight ship, kept payroll under budget. But this new guy, he wanted everything optimized to the decimal point. We had to start forecasting foot traffic based on year-over-year meteorological data! I mean, I sell home goods and apparel, I'm not running NASA. \n\nSo, I was spending hours, I mean absolutely agonizing hours, in the back office, staring at these spreadsheets, trying to make the payroll numbers match his impossible targets. And because of that, yeah, I suppose my mood did change. Susan definitely mentioned I was bringing the work home with me more than usual. I’d be sitting at the dinner table on a Tuesday, eating our meatloaf, and my mind would just be racing, calculating overtime hours and shrink percentages instead of listening to her talk about her book club. I was definitely more irritable, maybe a bit shorter with my assistant managers when the truck was late. \n\nMy thoughts just felt... crowded, I guess you could say. Like there were too many tabs open on the computer at once, all because of this constant, unrelenting pressure from the district level. But I just thought that was normal managerial stress, you know? It's retail. It ebbs and flows. I didn't think it would lead to... well, to me sitting here having my words get all jumbled up and my mouth not doing what my brain tells it to. But if you're looking for a starting point for when things started feeling different, it’s been a solid eleven months of this pressure cooker building up.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any head injuries or concussions recently?\n\nPatient: Head injuries? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I know exactly why you'd ask that, with the speech thing happening, it makes perfect sense you'd want to check the hardware, so to speak. But no, I haven't hit my head. I'm actually incredibly careful about that sort of thing. You kind of have to be when you work in retail management, especially when you spend as much time in the receiving bay and the stockrooms as I do. \n\nWe have these massive steel shelving units back there, industrial racking, you know? And they go all the way up to the twenty-foot ceilings, stacked with heavy merchandise—everything from boxed patio furniture to those dense seasonal displays that weigh an absolute ton. Safety is basically my middle name at this point. I'm the one who runs the mandatory safety huddles every single month for the staff. We go over OSHA compliance, three points of contact on the ladders, how to properly operate the manual pallet jacks... \n\nI mean, just last week I actually had to pull aside one of our new hires, a nice college kid named Tyler, because he was trying to pull a heavy box of ceramic planters off a top shelf by just standing on his tiptoes and tipping it forward instead of using the rolling staircase. I told him right then and there, I said, \"Tyler, that's exactly how you end up in the emergency room with a concussion, or worse, a fractured skull.\" So I am always, always hyper-aware of my surroundings. But as I started talking, my words just... they started jumping all over the place. \n\nI started out talking about the delivery trucks, which made sense, but then suddenly I was talking about Thursdays, because the trucks usually come on Thursdays, and then that made me think about the church grill we used last Thursday for the parish picnic, and before I knew it, I was rambling on about the tone my district manager used on our last conference call. And I could see it on Greg's face. He was just staring at me, you know? That look people give you when they have absolutely no idea how to follow what you're saying, like you're speaking a foreign language or you've completely lost the plot. \n\nAnd the frustrating part is, in my head, the connection between the inventory, the trucks, the schedule, and my boss makes perfect sense! It’s all part of the same stressful situation. But when it comes out of my mouth, it just... it doesn't connect for anyone else. It's like I'm trying to hand someone a neatly organized stack of papers, but right as I hand it over, a gust of wind blows them all over the room, and they're just left holding one random page about a church grill while I'm trying to explain payroll. I wouldn't even know where to find them if I wanted to, which I certainly do not. \n\nYou have to understand, in my line of work, you have to be sharp. I'm fifty-nine now, I got my business degree back in the late eighties, and honestly, even back then in college, I was always the designated driver. I was the one making sure my buddies got home safe because I just never saw the appeal of losing control like that. \n\nAnd especially now, with this new district manager breathing down my neck about labor margins and shrink... I mean, if I were drinking heavily or doing drugs, I'd have been fired six months ago. I need all my faculties just to keep the seasonal aisle transitions straight. I actually had to let a guy go a few years back, a night stocker, because he came in smelling like a brewery, and I told him right to his face that we run a professional environment here and safety is paramount.
